title: Functions Part 3: Outputs & Return Values
summary: Covers functions that send a value back with return, capturing that value in a variable, and splitting work into small functions (calcBottles, calcChange) whose outputs feed other code. Ends by making the price a parameter too.

concepts.heading: The return keyword
points: A function can take input (parameters) and give output (a return value); this is the third kind of function after no-input and with-input.
Place return followed by an expression as the last statement; the value becomes the result of the call expression.
Capture it by assigning the call to a variable: var change = getMilk(4); the right-hand side is replaced by the returned value.
Without a return statement the call only runs the body and produces no useful value (it evaluates to undefined).
Demo: return money % 1.5 gives the leftover cash; 4 with bottles at 1.5 gives 1, 3 gives 0.
(Extra) return also ends the function immediately, so nothing after it in the same path runs.

concepts.heading: Composing functions
points: Move a self-contained calculation into its own function, e.g. calcBottles(startingMoney, costPerBottle) that returns the number of bottles.
A function call can be used inside another expression, e.g. concatenated in a log string; when execution reaches it the engine runs the function and substitutes the returned value.
Arguments are matched by position: first argument to first parameter, second to second.
Do the same for change: calcChange(startingAmount, costPerBottle) returns startingAmount % costPerBottle, and getMilk can return calcChange(...) as its output.
Print the result with a message by calling getMilk inside console.log and concatenating a string.
Making cost a parameter of getMilk as well removes the hard-coded 1.5: getMilk(10, 3) works with new prices without editing the maths.

concepts.heading: Modulo recap
points: Modulo gives the remainder, so spending on whole bottles leaves money % price as change, e.g. 5 with price 1.5 gives 0.5.

pitfalls: Calling a function and ignoring its return value when you needed it.
Forgetting return so the variable becomes undefined.
Swapping argument order when a function has several parameters.
Floating point output such as 0.5 change is fine here but decimals can show tiny errors in other calculations.
Reference repo diverges: it passes change and bottles into getMilk and builds a message rather than returning change; also leaves a non-English variable name, which was renamed in the snippet above.
